I suggest in the context that "ZK" probably stands for Joint Command -- "for Kosovo and Metohija on the 19th and 20th of September, 1998, I informed you personally by phone or decision to form those intervention forces." So you don't know when the order came from the President. And I take it that's President Milosevic. You don't know exactly when that order was issued, do you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of what you are asking me, sir, I don't know. I understood that it was my task to assist the Chamber by saying what I know. But with Their Honours' leave, the beginning of item 2 says quite unambiguously that the decision is contained in the plan approved by the President. I don't know precisely when the plan was drawn up, who drew it up, whether it was in the President's office or the General Staff, but I beg that we not only read the last sentence but, if you insist on this, that we also read the beginning of item 2, which tells me that there was in existence a plan approved by the President of the State which contained that decision of his. That's my reading of item 2 in the Serbian language. But I really didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Bakrac on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just to add something to the transcript. Page 48, line 10: "A lot of what you're asking me about, I don't know." The witness said: "A lot of what you're asking me about in 1998, I don't know." So the year 1998 has been left out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if you would go on and read the last paragraph under item number 2, it says: "As part of the conclusions from the ZK" - I say Joint Command - "for Kosovo and Metohija meeting, I sent you the decision to form rapid-intervention forces, which you forbade in your order, number" such-and-such. Now, let me go to another exhibit, jumping ahead of where I wanted to, but I think it pertains to this. General Pavkovic says on his return from the reporting session with the Joint Command of the 19th and 20th of September --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like look at Exhibit P1468. And in English it's page 121, and in the B/C/S the ERN, last four digits, are 8518, which I believe would be page 47, but I'm not fully confident of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Actually, General, I can give you hard copies of the next couple of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This page reflects a meeting of the 19th of September, 1998, the Joint Command. And the first person to speak on that occasion appears to be you, General Lazarevic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first thing under your name is an acronym with the letters translated in English as "NVOR prepared in 5 villages," and it names Lipovac, Grcin, and Kales. Can you tell us what "NVOR" stands for?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This abbreviation contains an error. It's a typing letter in the last letter. It means "weapons and military equipment." But this last letter "R," I don't know what it might refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you read -- read out the Serbian. Maybe we can hear what it should be in English. Just read out those four letters.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NVOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say they should be, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they were referring to what I gather from the context, the last letter should be "P," rather than "R". "Weapons and military equipment." But I really don't know what it says really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, simply to draw attention to the following: In the English version, although it's gone off the screen now, the sentence begins with an abbreviation; however, in the Serbian version there seems to be a word before the abbreviation which does not appear in the English. So in the Serbian version, in front of this abbreviation there is a word; whereas, in English it begins with the abbreviation. And there is a mistranslation after this abbreviation. So it might be best if we were to have the entire sentence interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, could you read out that entire sentence for us, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Gathering" -- it's abbreviated, but it probably refers to gathering or collecting -- "weapons and military equipment in five villages, Lipovac, Grcin, Kabas [as interpreted]" and so on, "50 barrels."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that makes sense, I guess, because the next sentence has been translated as: "More weapons have been surrendered in Rajkovici"; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would read this with some difficulty. "In the village of Papracani." I don't know about the village of Rajkovici. I do know about a village called Papracani. It's a "P," the first letter, not an "R." 13 barrels, hand-held launchers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the rest of what I read was correct. It said "more weapons have been surrendered"; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if you can just turn to the next page, I want to -- I want to show that the document reflects that apparently General Pavkovic was also present at that meeting on the 19th of September. You see a reference to him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you speak a second time apparently. What I have translated here are parts of what General Pavkovic say are illegible. But there's one sentence translated as: "We have to see what we are going to do with the civilians." Do you see that? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we -- we might zoom in. It might be better if we zoomed in on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This other second word is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- "Morimor" [as interpreted]. It says "place."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it's the last entry under "General Pavkovic" that has the time reference of 1200 ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what you mean, yes. "Let's see what we will do with the civilians," probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you are listed a second time at this meeting. But then I'd like to go to the next page, which is 8520 for you; page 123 in the English. We'll have to rotate that. Yes. And it appears the first speaker at that meeting is General Pavkovic; correct? Talking about preparation for the action -- Action Cicavica.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cicavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall, did you attend this meeting? Your name does not appear, but I will tell you you are listed as appearing on the following day, the 21st, and you were at the meeting on the 19th. I'm -- I'm just wondering if you recall whether or not you also attended on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember and I don't believe that whoever wrote this would not mention my presence. At the beginning, he says who is present, as you can see, and I really don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the tendency not to list who's absent, rather than who's present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would say that nobody knows who was supposed to be present, because it was an ad hoc gathering. Whoever turned up, turned up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just answer my question, Mr. Lazarevic. Is it not your experience from these that generally speaking they note who is absent at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't have any contemporaneous experience. But I've seen documents showing that it's not as you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where it says who is present and who is absent. That's my experience from reviewing these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, which one are you referring to when you say that at the beginning it says who is present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the Prosecutor has those documents on those several occasions I attended, I remember it says "present," and then it lists some names and "Colonel Lazarevic." I remember that. So it lists certain names, including "Colonel Lazarevic." As to the date, I don't know. It's probably the date mentioned by the Prosecutor. But I am trying to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we have one in that form, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, the first appearance --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The first one I have is at page 68 of the English. It's a meeting of the 23rd of August. And it's page 8470 for the B/C/S. I can -- I can read it out, Your Honour. It says -- it lists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. No, no, the reference is good enough for me. It's just the one on the screen gives us the people absent, and I wonder what the position is in relation to the 21st and the 19th that you've been asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, there -- I would say there's not one entirely consistent procedure throughout. On the 23rd, it lists three people as not being present: Minic -- not being present: Mr. Minic, Matkovic, and Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Matkovic. And then it does list as present Obrad Stevanovic and Colonel B. Lazarevic. But Pavkovic, Djordjevic, Djordjevic, Gajic, Sainovic are also present at that meeting but not listed as being present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you know that from the record of what they are alleged to have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the reference that you've just given sounds like a reference to others attending who are not regular members, which would -- would fit the evidence that Mr. Lazarevic has given.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That appears to be his first appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would ask you to look at the next page, General. I think it's 8521. It's still continuing on in that meeting of the 20th. And although I know you were not listed as being particularly present at that meeting and you don't recall if you were, I want to ask you if what I have in my English translation under Mr. Sainovic's first bullet point is correct. It's translated as: "To prepare units for faster interventions." Can you read that? Or would it help if we enlarge it on the monitor for you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in a little bit so that I am able to read what it says exactly. "Prepare and train units" -- "a unit." "A unit for rapid intervention."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then if we could go to the next page. And I believe these are the notes for the meeting of the 21st of September. The English translation says "01/09." But I would suggest to Your Honours that looking at the B/C/S that looks like "21" to me, and it's also consistent in terms of where it appears in the document, that is, between the 20th and the 22nd. And, General, you're listed -- specifically listed as attending this one. It says: "Absent." It says: "All attended, General Lazarevic as well." Do you recall this meeting on the 21st of September?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I attended. I don't know whether the date is correct. If it's -- if that's what it says here, then probably it is. But if you want me to confirm the time and the date, I can't do that. But I would like to draw Your Honours' attention to the fact that it says here "not present," and it is also listed "and General Lazarevic." And this is what I meant -- or rather, "everybody is present, including General Lazarevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. And, General, in addition to these two meetings that we talked about, that you're listed as being present, for the 19th and 21st of September, you are also listed ... Well, let's -- I'm sorry. Let's go to page 8516. This is page 119 of the English and over, actually, onto 120. It's a meeting for the 18th of September. Do you have that page, General? I may not have given you that many.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I'm actually trying to find my way around these papers. And if you can give me a minute or two -- no, I don't have anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't. Because I started out by talking about the 19th and 20th. So let me give you two more pages, with the help of the usher. And let's start with the first one, which has 8514. It's a meeting of the 17th of September. And in the English this is page 117. Do you find that one, General? September 17th.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You gave me the one for the 18th of September, not the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have it. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the 17th, it lists as absent Mr. Matkovic. And then in English we need to go to page 119, which is a continuation of this meeting on the 17th. And it's on the second page for you, General, I think.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It lists you as speaking, but you're not listed particularly as attending that meeting; correct? You are listed as speaking and you're talking about "Last month our border posts had been attacked six times. Part of the Military Police Battalion was engaged. The plan for Saturday and Sunday is to disarm the village of Damjane." So it appears you were at that meeting on the 17th but there's no specific listing of you in those attending; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what this paper indicates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since my colleague Mr. Hannis referred the witness to another page, but I think that he should refer him back to page 1 so that he can look at that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you can look at any page you want concerning this meeting on -- on the 17th. I don't see anywhere where, regarding the list of people attending or being absent, that you're mentioned, but I do see you speaking on -- on the last page. Does that -- is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any comments as to who was present in the introductory part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If you could go, then, to the next document, for the 18th of September, 1998. And in English it's best to look at page 120, which has the starting time and lists those absent. It's -- it's translated as Mr. Mijac, Mr. Sainovic, and General "illegible." In the Serbian, in the original, General, are you able to help us with the names of those absent? Because to me it looks like the first one is Gospodin Minic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I read it, as far as I'm able on this piece of paper. Mr. Sainovic, yes. And I think it says "General Lukic," if I'm reading this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That -- that seems to make sense and that looks consistent to me as well, General, but there's no one -- you are not listed as -- as being particularly present at this meeting, but you appear to be the first one to speak; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here on this paper, as I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So from this document, it appears that you attended four meetings in September. Does that refresh your recollection now about how many meetings you attended of the Joint Command in September 1998? Because when you testified, it was unclear to me, but I -- I thought you only recalled attending a couple of meetings in September and one in August.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I said something else. And let me just say, on some occasions, not at some meetings. I did not specify the number of meetings. I said that I think I was there once in August and once in September, when I stayed there a couple of days. Now, as to the number of times - because I stayed in Pristina for a few days in September - I don't recall having specified the number of meetings that I attended with the corps commander, meetings with the people from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, for the record, Your Honour, I would indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the question hasn't been answered. The question was: Does this refresh your memory and help you to confirm that you attended at least four meetings in September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what it says here, that would appear to be so. But I really cannot confirm whether on those days I was there. There's no reason for us if anybody wrote -- if somebody wrote that down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there might be two ways of doing that. Did you keep some -- did you keep some sort of -- I'm sorry. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but it seems to me that Mr. Hannis first showed the minutes from August. And -- and I'm afraid that now this is referred to as a September meeting. I would kindly like to ask my learned colleague Mr. Hannis to check that, but I believe that the first minutes that were referred to were -- were from August and now we have the 17th, the 18th, and the 21st. I'm not sure about all that. But if perhaps my colleague Mr. Hannis might assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm only concerned with September at the moment and the record shows the 17th, 18th, 19th, and 21st so far. And these are the four that I'm referring to, not August. And I want to ask you now, Mr. Lazarevic: Did you keep some sort of personal record or diary during this period of your movements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I did not. Definitely not. No records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would there be within the corps a record of your movements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm almost sure that there were no such records. But if -- now, whether anyone kept any records about my movements, this is something that is really hard to believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, presumably during the war, the war diary would tell us where you were on each individual day. And this is -- I appreciate this is before the war, but during the war would -- would the record not show where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, not necessarily so, because those details are not entered, not even in the combat report, which is a document which is much more detailed. I never saw anyone note that down at the corps command. I saw that the subordinate units would note down my arrival, but not at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's look at it a different way. You've now been able to see these entries in the document which is P1468, and you're a man who has a good recollection of the events of the time. Are these entries consistent with things that you would be likely to have reported at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really cannot remember saying things that are quoted here in the bullet points, in the number of bullet points that exist here. And in particular, that -- the way that this is recorded, in one of those papers it is stated that I spoke about the Cicavica plan. This is not in the border belt at all, so I really didn't deal with that at all. Secondly, I read something about Budakovo here, that some things had to be blocked there. And I recall quite clearly this was a special situation. That it -- the way it is presented here is the exact opposite of the actual facts. And if we -- if you allow me now to find this in -- among the papers, I can be even more specific. This is just what I was able to ascertain in -- by a cursory look. So I really couldn't confirm that the person who kept the record, the recording secretary, really wrote down everything as it should have been written down. At least, as far as my words are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Subject to the questions that are asked of you in cross-examination and re-examination, I am likely to return to this issue and -- and ask you more later, but do you go as far as to say someone has fabricated entries about things and attributed them to you, when you never said them? That this is a false document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not prepared to make an assessment of this document in one way or another, so I'm not saying that this is a forgery or that this was actually produced at the time. I am not qualified to do so. But I noticed two things in this very brief period of time that I absolutely did not say. Somebody else may have said that and then it was attributed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, with regard to -- I think you mentioned Budakovo. Allowing for the possibility that whoever wrote the notes down may have misinterpreted what you said, did -- did you speak about Budakovo in any of those meetings in September? Do you remember talking about that village?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not talking about the village. I was talking about the Jezerska mountains, and there are some 20 villages there, including Budakovo. But I said that some radio deceptive operations should be carried out against those terrorist forces deployed there. It is tactical or operational, camouflage or ruse-type of operations. So it has nothing to do with any kind of combat actions. This is what I meant when I indicated that a couple of moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you saying you didn't mention the name of that village? You can recall now years later specifically that you did not use the name of that village in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that you're really asking too much of me. I remember the Jezerska mountains. I don't recall this village as such. But I remember this kind of -- this radio training, the radio camouflage training that was supposed to be carried out there. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, did you in preparation for your testimony, or otherwise -- just out of curiosity, did you look at Exhibit P1468, the meetings of the Joint Command in 1998? Did you review that before you testified here?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes., I did review all that, but not in such great detail, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You must have anticipated that you were going to be asked questions about the Joint Command and whether or not you had attended any meetings. You did expect that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have replied and I am replying, whether I attended or not. So I really was prepared to do -- to do all that, but I was not expecting that I would be asked to review every single word or to even try and decode it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, did you, in reviewing it, look through to see what meetings you were at, to help refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have a look, but I did not make any notes or records. This is what I was able to recall even before I read those documents, that I attended those meetings twice. And this is what I had to say in answer to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me go back to the first time that I'm aware of you talking about "Joint Command" in -- and whether you attended any meetings or not. Do you recall being interviewed by -- by mostly Mr. Coo, Phil Coo, investigator Annette Murtagh, and I was present for some of your interviews, as well as Ms. Moeller for a portion. You recall those interviews in, I think it was, March 2005, shortly after you arrived here; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is Exhibit P950. And I'm sorry, General, it's only in English. The videotape is on DVDs and CDs. But let me ask you the question and we'll -- we'll go from there. Mr. Coo was asking you about the Joint Command. And at page 72, line 8, you say: "I do not know how to explain precisely what a Joint Command is." In line 11, you say: "Throughout the most of 1998, I was in Djakovica." And at line 13: "I was far away from the command of the Pristina Corps." Do you agree with all that so far?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go any further, Mr. Hannis, are we on to this composite document you gave us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of the page number. It should be page 72, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- in the lower right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The -- oh, yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at line 16, you say: "This group of men and myself in Djakovica were isolated." And at line 19: "It was only twice during 1998 that I travelled, and that by helicopter, because the roads couldn't be used. I travelled to Pristina for a short time, once to be appointed general, which was in September; and the second time, for a very short while in October after the OSCE Mission's arrival and Walker, because I had to report to the commander." And then you go on and say, even though you said only twice, you go on at line 24 and say: "And the third time I was lucky enough to be flown in a helicopter to Nis to visit my family." So when you were interviewed in March 2005, you said you only went to Pristina twice in 1998, once to be appointed general, in September; and the second time, for a report to the commander in connection with the OSCE. And then when you testified earlier this week -- or last week, I'm sorry, at page 17820, Judge Bonomy was asked you some questions because there -- there was some uncertainty about how many meetings you went to. And at line 7, you say: "Your Honour, when I say 'occasions,' I'm referring to one occasion in August and another -- or the other in September. But in September I spent two or three days in Pristina and in August I spent only one day. In August I attended one meeting, and September, on those two or three days, I attended two meetings. Out of those two meetings, I cannot confirm whether I took the floor every time." So what was it that refreshed your memory between the interview in March, when you make no mention of going to Pristina for these meetings, and your testimony last week, when you recalled one in August and two in September? Was it from having looked at the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Bakrac on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the interpretation that we and the accused got was, "When you never said that you attended the meetings." And that is not correct. This is not what the accused had said. And I would like us all to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this is what the interpretation is, and it's for the witness to deal with issues like this, not you, by intervening. There is an accurate translation of that. And the question is a perfectly proper question. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do I -- I need to repeat that? What was it that --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would be so kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the interview in March 2005 you didn't -- you said you only went to Pristina twice during 1998: One, to be appointed a general; and the second time, regarding reporting to the commander about OSCE. In your testimony last week, you mentioned going once in August, and another occasion in September for two or three days during which you attended two meetings. So one meeting in August and two in September. What was it that refreshed your memory between March 2005 and testifying last week about attending those meetings; one in August, two in September?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in that interview I did say that I attended on two occasions the meetings in Pristina with the corps commander, with the people from the police force, and with some state officials. I wasn't correct enough about the time. I spoke about September and October as two occasions. But if you ask me now what refreshed my memory, I would say that I have looked at this list and I saw that it was not September and October. October is something that does not have to do with this meeting; it has to do with the OSCE mission. There was one occasion in August instead and another occasion in September. We can't see it from this segment of the transcript, but this whole story that took 10 or 15 minutes contains what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you haven't answered my question. Are you saying my question is mistaken because in the interviews you talked about attending those meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, maybe you can help me find it. Let me go on. On page 73 of your interview - maybe this is what you're thinking of - at the very bottom of page 72, you say: "I knew that a special group." And on top of page 73: "Team of men, both from the Federal and Republic's government were engaged in this political dialogue. I knew the names of these men and sometimes saw them. That was Sainovic, Minic, Andjelkovic, Matkovic, Lilic, Defence Minister Bulatovic. And this group of men, either individually or in group, were those who came most often to Metohija, where I spent most of 1998." You mean in Djakovica; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. "I occasionally saw them, but not all of them together, just one or two of them when they came to Metohija, and this was with -- together with the corps commander, army commander, or the chief of General Staff. They toured the most jeopardized parts of the state border." And then you mention a couple of visits to the state border and Mr. Lilic. At line 18, you say: "I also had information that this group of politicians frequently visited Kosovo, more precisely Pristina, and that they had meetings with the army commander, with the Pristina Corps Command, and the MUP HQ in Pristina in order to receive information..." So in the interview you told us you knew about there were some of the kinds of meetings like that of this body that I call "the Joint Command," but you don't say anything there about you attending any of those meetings, do you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this part. Not in this passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is that not what he went on to say immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And he says: "I cannot remember the exact day, but it was definitely in October."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is line 23. "At the request of Corps Command General Pavkovic, I came to the barracks in Pristina by helicopter. My task was to brief him about the situation at the state border after disengagement of the main part of the army forces upon the arrival of the OSCE. And on that day, that evening, a meeting was held where information was exchanged. That was the first time I ever saw a larger group of these men, three or four men from the police, several of them from the political ranks." And this is in October, and we've been talking about meetings between July and September. And he talked about meetings in August and September.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, my colleague Mr. Hannis is suggesting that the accused has never said that. Now he's saying he didn't say it about July. Whereas, the accused began his answer by saying, "Yes, I was mistaken. I see it was August and September, not September and October, as I had said previously." My learned friend Mr. Hannis just suggested that he had never said it in -- in the interview and then proceeded to read the passage in -- in the interview where he did say it. And this is simply confusing the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I -- I disagree with you, Mr. Bakrac, I'm afraid. And it's a matter you can take up in re-examination, subject to the reference to July, which is strictly accurate but could be said to be misleading, because it's a reference to "between July and September." There's nothing in there that's, in my opinion, inappropriate, so I repel your objection. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, General, at -- taken at best, during your interview it seems like you talked about attending one meeting in October when you came in connection with the OSCE matter where there were some three or four men from the police and also state security and several from the political ranks. Do you recall at that October meeting who was present? Because I will -- I will tell you - and we can -- we can check this, if you want - but if you look at the Joint Command meeting notes, I see no reference to you at any October meetings recorded in Exhibit P1468. So who was at the meeting you are talking about in October? Do you recall any specific persons? And can you tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that precisely or imprecisely. I know only what I said, a group of people. I really cannot tell you the names. My best recollection of that interview leads me to ask the Trial Chamber to look at the transcript more carefully. The interview on this topic took a long time. I must have said more. I cannot follow this on the screen now. I firmly believe that it was not quite accurately presented here, in terms of my answers to the questions when, how many times I was in Pristina. I recognise what I see here, but I remember having said more on this specific issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I -- I appreciate what you're saying, Mr. Lazarevic, but it appears - and this is hopefully a clarification for Mr. Bakrac also - it appears you acknowledge you were at one meeting in August, at least two meetings in September, and that in October you were also in Pristina in connection with the OSCE and that there was a meeting then also. Is that a fair summary of what is not in dispute now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is so. I'm just saying that I remember this part of the interview differently. I'm sorry, Your Honour. This meeting in October did not relate to coordination with the police and that whole story from the previous time. It had to do with the OSCE. That was a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. And I appreciate there are also many matters in dispute. I was trying to identify what wasn't in dispute to make sure that Mr. Hannis is not misleading you in any way, and I think that confirms that the questions have not been misleading, although a different gloss may be put on the matter by re-examination. You -- you, I take it, have access to the original of this interview. You must have the recording of it available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The accused has neither the translation or the -- nor the recording, because he does not have a laptop. He is not able to operate a laptop. So he has neither the translation nor the DVD. I was waiting for Mr. Hannis to use this exhibit to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a -- a written B/C/S version of this interview? No. It's simply on the DVD.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And that was furnished to the Defence sometime ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. There's no complaint about that. Just give me a moment, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As you know, Mr. Lazarevic, it's very important there should be no contact between you and any party involved in this case, any of your representatives or anyone else's while you're giving evidence. On the other hand, there's no reason why you cannot, overnight, be looking at material which refreshes your memory or clarifies things for you. And we shall do all we can - and I think it will be possible to arrange for you to have a DVD player at the weekend for delivery of the DVDs to you - and then you -- I appreciate it's lengthy, but I imagine you've enough recollection of the interview to be able to identify the batch you ought to focus on in refreshing your memory so when you come back on Monday you're in a position to tell us anything you want to add, to ensure that your position is not misunderstood. Now, Mr. Bakrac, is that an acceptable arrangement to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, it's 21 or 22 hours of footage. And second, I don't know how and whether it will be organised, because Mr. Lazarevic does not have a laptop. He doesn't use one. I don't know how that can be organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I -- I presume these are in DVD format and can be used in a player. I -- the Chamber would also have no objection to you compiling a list of the points on the DVDs that you think he ought to concentrate on and passing that to him, since you think, you know -- and I agree with you, going over the whole thing is unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my -- my case manager just informed me it's his opinion that it does need to be a laptop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It won't work on a simple DVD player.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But we would try the identify, at least as regarding page 72 and 73, where they are time-wise on the DVD. However, I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If others can do the same. And I'm sure we can find a way of providing the necessary assistance. Because the alternative would be to go through it in court, which would be Mr. Lazarevic's right. And that's in no one's interest if there's another way of doing it. So we'll adjourn now and resume at five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis. Oh, sorry, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, I wish to make an objection to the use of this document, the interview of Mr. Lazarevic, and I wish to draw your attention to page 3 of the transcript, last paragraph, where the Office of the Prosecutor when this interview was being discussed and agreed upon, the OTP promised to furnish a transcript. That transcript and the interview itself are of equal importance as the indictment and the judgement. All of them have to be supplied in a language the accused understands. This interview, he does not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One second. Where is the provision that the transcript has to be provided in a language that he understands? If you direct me to the Rule that provides for that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not written. It is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the transcript is evidence. This transcript is evidence, and it exists only in a language the accused does not understand. And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. The evidence is the interview recording. The recording is available in a language he understand, because he spoke it in his own language. And it was translated on the tape -- the questions were translated into his language on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally, Your Honour, the accused, who should be in the most favourable position, is in the most unfavourable position in this courtroom because we have all received one copy of the transcript and we are able to follow what Mr. Hannis is indicating and what he's saying; the accused being the only person not being able to locate in the transcript the passage they are asking him about and that he needs to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you intend to continue at the moment with this line of examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was in a bit of a quandary about that, but I tell you what I have. We have -- we have the video loaded at the point where this discussion took place. We could play that entire two or three pages. I have to tell you it's about 10 minutes or 12 minutes long. We could do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But do you want to -- is that what you want to do just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I would like to do that, Your Honour, and I think we can see if there's any confusion or misunderstanding about what's transpiring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the interview record is already admitted as an exhibit in this trial, so this objection is far too late; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's my position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. And the transcript, is it -- does it accompany the -- the interview record as part of the process so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think originally when this exhibit was admitted, it was the English transcript that was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's what's been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And when we recently -- the other day when we asked to put in the numbered-page version of the English transcript, we also sought your permission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- at that point to include the CD or the DVD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And there was no objection at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Now, Mr. Bakrac, why has this not been raised before?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend Mr. Hannis just explained that he only subsequently announced that he would not tender but use this. And as soon as he began to use it, I objected. The English version was admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's -- that's quite inaccurate. The transcript is part of the Prosecution case. The transcript is relied upon by the Prosecution. It is admitted. No objection was taken. The matter arose again the other day, yesterday, when the Prosecutor tendered this composite document with all the parts of the interview in it, asked for that to be substituted for the other transcripts, and added the CDs or DVDs recording it, and you took no objection. Now, it's in. There's no objection taken by you. It's in without objection. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we objected that the interview really took place and the original of the CDs are really authentic -- sorry, we didn't object to that. But we object to using it because the accused cannot follow it in that language, because he doesn't have the transcript in the language he understands before him. And I invoke the practice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis is going to follow a different practice and he's going to show him it, in his own language, on the screen. Now, do you object to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know which passage he will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The passage we've been exploring already. It takes 10 minutes to view it, unfortunately but we will have to do it that way, in fairness to Mr. Lazarevic. If you're unhappy about the transcript on its own being used, then that's the course we will follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't object to the accused viewing the DVD, but I would like the transcript to be before him in a language he understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's just not going to happen, and you know it's impractical and you know that if you wanted that to happen, you should have asked for it long ago. So let's proceed, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just very briefly want to kind of round out the record, because you may not know this. The -- I'm quite certain all the rest of the accused who gave statements to the OTP received transcripts in B/C/S. I think Mr. Lazarevic is the only one who didn't get his transcript in B/C/S. And I don't know if that makes a difference to -- about anything, but I think it at least ought to be in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The difference it makes is that it surprises me nothing has been done about it until today. Proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. It's my understanding from my case manager, that this is -- this is in sections -- Sanction. I'm sorry. This is in Sanction. And we're going to start -- I think this is at 1 hour, 50 minutes, 30 seconds, and it is the beginning of page 72 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "VL: I think that Mr. Coo is trying to ask me something very specific. I don't know whether I can explain it well, but I'll try. I want to be completely sincere, because in my assessment, I believe that you are trying to ask me whether there was a Joint Command, because I did hear of this term being used in the course of 1998 and I did -- but I did also hear -- I have also heard of a coordination body, but this was in 2000 and 2001, and it involved the south of Serbia. "My initial answer to you and a very sincere one is I cannot -- I do not know how to explain precisely what a Joint Command is. I have also read in the indictment that I was a member of this Joint Command in 1998. But if you'll allow me, if I may recall, throughout most of 1998 I was in Djakovica with a small group of men from the Pristina Corps near the state border with Albania. So I was far away from the command of the Pristina Corps, which was in Pristina, and even farther away from some other possible potential commands. "This may not be a good -- a good thing for me to say as a soldier, but this group of men and myself in Djakovica were isolated not only by the tasks of defending the border day and night but also de facto, because we were encircled by terrorist forces. As far as I can remember, it was only twice during 1998 that I travelled, and that by helicopter, because the roads couldn't be used. I travelled to Pristina for a short time. Once to be appointed general, which was in September, and the second time for a very short while in October after -- after the OSCE mission's arrival and Walker, because I had to report to the commander. And the third time I was also lucky enough to be flown in a helicopter to Nis to visit my family. "To this day I do not know, haven't heard of, and have not seen an order which appoints me as a member of this body which some call the Joint Command, and until a year and a half ago I never even thought of this. Luckily I didn't put much thought into this, even at the time in 1998, or not -- whether such a body existed or not. And now specifically what I did know then and what I do know today, I knew that in mid-1998 Serbia tried by political means to prevent terrorism and war. I knew that a political dialogue was -- was established with Albanian representatives. I knew that a special group, team of men, both from the Federal and Republic's government were engaged in this political dialogue. I knew the names of these mens and -- men and sometimes saw them. These were Sainovic, Minic, Andjelkovic, Matkovic, Lilic, Defence Minister Bulatovic, and this group of men either individually or in group were those who came most often to Metohija, where I spent most of 1998. "I occasionally saw them, but not all of them together. Just one or two of them, when they came to Metohija. And this was with -- together with the corps commander, army commander, or the chief of General Staff. They toured the most jeopardized parts of the state border. At the time, I thought this was a good thing and that it was better for politicians to do their job than for soldiers to -- to do -- to work. "In two visits to the state border I saw that they were -- they were very concerned about the situation but that they were also listening to our suggestions about the -- about expanding the -- the border belt. I refer specifically to Mr. Lilic, Zoran, who was at the time, as far as I -- I think, Deputy Prime Minister, Federal Government Deputy Prime Minister. "I also had information that this group of politicians frequently visited Kosovo, more precisely Pristina, and that they had meetings with the army commander, with the Pristina Command -- Pristina Corps Command and the MUP HQ in Pristina in order to receive information about the situation in the field and the situation in the army and the police. I cannot remember the precise date, but it was definitely in October. At the request of corps commander General Pavkovic I came to the barracks in Pristina by helicopter. My task was to brief him about the situation at the state border after the disengagement of the main part of the army forces upon the arrival of the OSCE mission. And on that day, that evening, a meeting was held where information was exchanged. As far as I remember, at the building of the provincial executive council. That was the first -- that was the first time that I saw a larger group of these men, three or four men from the police, several of them from the political ranks. When I say "police," I also mean state security. And all I can say is that after this briefing, the situation and the information was very bleak. Because around 2.000 OSCE verifiers and observers had arrived, but terrorist operations did not end but escalated in Kosovo --"

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the point at which I intended to stop, Your Honour, unless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- there's a request to hear any more of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you had a chance to watch and listen to that. Did you -- did you hear anything in the -- in the translation that you have a problem with now?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I have no problem with what I heard. What I have a problem with is either my recollection or something that cannot be seen today in the general context. And that's what I'm saying. What I'm saying is that on that topic, over those five or so days with the investigator, we talked at least on two occasions. We discussed it at least twice. And I remember that I spoke in greater detail about my travel to Pristina and my attendance at some of those meetings and briefings, not only the October one. That is the essence of what I was trying to say before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a record of that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I honestly don't know. What I have are some summaries prepared by one of my investigators regarding where certain topics were talked about, including Joint Command. And I have noted those on -- on a list that my case manager has been working on. And I -- I don't know how best to do this, Your Honour. In terms of the transcript, we have a copy of the transcript where we've noted at the top of each page the hour and minute at which that page begins, but that's not a lot of help to Mr. Lazarevic, because it's on the English transcript. So I -- I guess I'm just advising the Court and Mr. Bakrac of that in case there's a way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it must assist if it -- if it gives the hour and minute at which the extract starts, because the extract is what he wants to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, well, we do have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in terms of if he wants to look at anything else in the interview, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed. Indeed. But it allows him to identify the parts. And Mr. Bakrac has been given the same facility to identify parts that he wants him to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, then. But I will -- I will leave the interview for today and go on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to show you next Exhibit P1440. And I can give you a hard copy of this one as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is Exhibit P1440. It is a annex to the report regarding incidents resulting in death and use of critical ammunition from the Pristina Corps Command, General Pavkovic, to the 3rd Army forward command post. Did you see this document before today in preparing for your evidence or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it was shown once in e-court by one of the Defence teams, but I never held it in my hands. I viewed it for a few seconds. Then I recognised the events discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That -- that answered my next question. In item 2, it says: "Based on combat reports, regular intelligence reports, and written reports by the -- all unit commanders of 5 October 1998, the Pristina Corps Command does not have information about the alleged massacre against the civilian population in Gornje Obrinje." You were aware of that event at that time, weren't you, that that was -- that was something that was being discussed rather broadly, this allegation of a massacre of civilians in Gornje Obrinje? You heard about it at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the order of the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Pavkovic, addressed to all units to make additional checks in all units and all -- and all reports on the engagement of units and to report back to the commander whether units have any more information regarding these reports, but I don't know whether these reports were first made by the media or where they came from. I didn't see them at the time. I know only about the order of the Pristina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in connection with that, General Pavkovic says that also: "In the period while the plan for fighting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija from 25 July until 29 September 1998 was being implemented." My question is: General Lazarevic, at that time were -- were you aware of the plan for fighting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija? Had you held a copy of that plan in your hand in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not held a copy of the plan in my hand, but I knew it had been drawn up at the highest state military and political level in Belgrade and adopted. I didn't see the plan, nor did I hold it in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that not a document that -- it seems to me that's the document that you, as the Chief of Staff for the Pristina Corps Command and -- and the guy on the scene as the forward command post, should have had a copy of. Is that not right? Or is this -- is that something at too high a level for you to see?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put two questions to me. I will try to concentrate and focus, but I beg Their Honours not to hold it against me if I repeat. As Chief of Staff, I had a special mission in the defence of the state border and I did not participate in planning of -- in the planning of many activities at the level of the corps command. So my answer is "no," because I was carrying out a special task in a separate direction. And, I'm sorry, I've forgotten what your other question was. I do apologise. If you could repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I guess --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, that I ask a double question this late in the day in the week. Is -- is the nature of this plan for fighting terrorism such that that's a document that would only be held and seen at the highest levels, such as at the Supreme Command Staff or maybe the 3rd Army level but would not come down to you in the forward command of the command post?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't like that. But the excerpt dealing with the border belt and the state border, yes. Not, however, the entire plan that the forward command post could have no influence on. I was near the border with a group of men in Djakovica and I couldn't influence planning or activities in the north of the province. Whatever related to the state border, yes, from the overall plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] From what we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From what we've heard in other evidence about this plan, it's been described as having five phases. Were you in 1998 aware of the fact that that plan had five phases?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, four, as far as I can remember. And later on a fifth phase was added on, to the best of my recollection. The initial plan had five phases and the -- had four phases and the fifth was added on later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of your earlier answers gives the impression that you were not aware of this plan at the time, and now you've said that you were aware of the fact that there were four phases. Now, what is the position, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is that I did not see the plan. I did not participate in its realization at the corps level. I don't know who drafted it. I only know it was done at the level of the top, state leadership, and I know that it was implemented in phases and that I participated in that part of the plan which related to the state border as Chief of Staff. That was the initial part of the plan, to protect the state border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, your answer was clear. There was part of it I couldn't see at the side of my screen. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, do you recall now what was the fifth phase that was added later to the original four?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't recall at present. Probably, I assume now, it might have to do with the flashpoint of the armed rebellion that remained in late September, but I really can't recall. I don't want to speculate. That what I recall, that there was some sort of fifth phase added on. I may be wrong. There may have been five from the outset, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that exist in written form as part of the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Pardon me, the ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The five-phase plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- I -- the evidence that I'm recalling are discussions about the plan at various places, including the Joint Command meetings, where there's a reference to "phases."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. But we know --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't recall a document that says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know there was something called Grom-1 and Grom-2 which relates to a similar -- mostly the same period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we are interested in the relationship between that and -- and the five-phase plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That -- that's where I'm going, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hannis. I just wanted to clarify one thing. Was -- if this plan was not available in its true shape, can that be constructed from the various documents? Have you been able to do it? Just -- just to ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for me it's a -- it's a continual work in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I know you talked before in your direct testimony about, I think, Grom-1 and -2 and -3 and maybe even a -4. I'm not sure. Can you tell us what is the relationship between Grom-1 and/or Grom-2 and what I've been referring to now as "the five-phase plan for combatting terrorism in Kosovo"? Are they distinct plans? Are they parts of the same plan? Can you tell us what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge concerning this is based, I have to admit, on what I heard in this courtroom. From Defence witnesses, the witnesses of the previous Defences, and, if I may continue, I understood that in 1998 there was a plan which was called Grom-98 and which contained two phases, Grom-98-1 and Grom-98-2, and that it was drawn up in the General Staff. The chief of the General Staff at that time was General Perisic. And this plan, Grom-98-1 and -2, mostly corresponds with the anti-terrorist actions of the police and army in 1998 over the longest period of time, but to the best of my recollection there was a small period in July where it does not correspond, and that's marked with a Roman numeral I, where -- where General Perisic in one or several sentences - I'm mentioning him because he was the chief of the General Staff - said that the previous activities had been implemented according to plan. I don't know what plan, but that's what I was able to understand in this courtroom. I did not go into an analysis of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Actually, I think that helps a little bit. I think we have a couple of 3D exhibits that pertain to this, Your Honour, but this late in the week in the day, I'd prefer to wait until Monday to tackle that. I have a couple more questions on this document, General, and then I think we'll conclude for the day. In this Exhibit P1440, item number 3 talks about the -- the kinds of ammunition -- the kinds of critical ammunition used. In your direct testimony, you explained something about a -- quantities of ammunition were measured in combat sets. Can -- can you elaborate on that for me a little bit. For example, 120-millimetre -- or 122-calibre ammunition, what -- how much constitute a combat set of that kind of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope Their Honours will not hold it against me if -- when I say that it depends on what sort of weapon we are talking about, because 122-millimetre ammunition is used in at least two kinds of weapons, sometimes it's 42 projectile, sometimes 48. I don't want to go into details, but it ranges from 42 to 48. Per artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So it -- 42 to 48 122-calibre, I would call them, "shells," it's translated as "bullet" here, but I would call that a shell.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what you might call it. That's what it's called in military terminology. I think it's written correctly here. I used the term "projectile" as a third possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So 42 to 48 would equal one combat set?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How about for 100-millimetre?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bullet of 100 millimetres is used also by an anti-tank gun or a gun mounted on a tank, of 100 millimetres. Yes. Well, now, I know for certain, as far as tanks go, that 48 projectiles apply, but I don't know about the gun, what combat set it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not necessarily a high point, could -- but could we end here for the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can end the evidence for the week, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two matters that we would like to deal with administratively. The first is -- of these is how the balance of time available for presentation of the Defence is to be utilised. And that's prompted by seeing that there are about 70 witnesses on Mr. Lazarevic's 65 ter list. There are 33 listed for November and December. It may be 33 is now the number intended to be called, since the indication was already firmly given that that case would be completed in December. However, the first three who are listed with the anticipated hours indicate no use is likely to be made of -- of 65 -- of 92 ter statements in their evidence, and indeed one of them -- in one case, the estimate for the length of examination-in-chief has increased. Now, Mr. Bakrac, we've a number of times commented that everyone has to try to tailor their case to fit. How is it you propose doing that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you observed quite correctly that from the time when we decided to call General Lazarevic as our first witness that we reduced our number of witnesses, because we believed that some things need not be repeated several times in court. So this is the list as it stands now. Depending on our -- the progress of our case, it may be further reduced but not substantially, we believe. That's number one. Number two, it appears to us that in the areas of some of the brigades where the Prosecution called a lot of evidence, that we have to focus on those areas and to devote more time to examination on those issues. We wanted to do so right at the beginning of our case. Number three, Your Honours, I understand that 140 hours was allotted to us to be divided between us and General Lukic's Defence, 70 hours each. We will endeavour to present our case within these limits, but I wanted to ask you one thing: At one point it was mentioned in this courtroom that no limits apply to the testimony of an accused. So my question is whether the time that we spend examining the accused is also a part of this allotment. With all our future witnesses, we will strive to use 92 ter statements or a combination of viva voce and 92 ter statements. As for this witness -- or rather, as for how we stand now, General Lazarevic's testimony is now in its second week. Mr. Cepic is now dealing with our next three witnesses. He might be able to tell us more about it, but these are witnesses that will deal with most of the evidence that has been called in this case. They were in the areas of -- of the brigades to which most of the evidence pertains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The overall total of 240 hours was based on the knowledge at that time that all -- not quite all but most of the accused were listed to give evidence. So it's assumed in that figure that the accused are giving evidence. What I was saying about the manner of the examination was that where we might make very pointed suggestions about how evidence could be better tailored in relation to some witnesses, we would not do so in relation to an accused unless it was obvious that -- that the Court was being abused in some way, and there's no question of that here. So that is part of your time. And indeed, on one view you've ended up with more time than you might have anticipated, because none of the accused preceding you has given evidence. Now, are you saying that you and the Lukic Defence have a -- an arrangement that the balance of the time would be split between you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we received an e-mail about two or three weeks ago. The calculation of the time from the Trial Chamber. I think it was Mr. Dawson, where -- where it said there are 140 hours left, do you have anything against dividing this time with the Lukic Defence, 70 hours each. We agreed to that, and we believed that this was -- this then settled the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you agree to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I have to ask my colleague whether a reply was sent to that e-mail. I will have to check whether we replied to that mail, to that e-mail. I can't now claim that, but we did reach an agreement on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the way we understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: An agreement with whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that the Lukic Defence agreed to that too, but I may be mistaken. That's the way I understood it, that they agreed to it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's sounding rather hazy. Let's hear from Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our understanding of how to divide the time is always based on the days and months. Our understanding is that Mr. Bakrac will end his -- or actually, that we -- General Lazarevic will end his defence by the end of this year; actually, by the Christmas break. And then we are going to start at the mid of January and we'll start [sic] in three months. That's our position from the beginning. And I think it's acceptable, knowing that we are the only police Defence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's a very general statement of the terms of discussions we have had. But as you know, the actual estimates are done in hours and you know what you've estimated and you know it's far, far in excess of even three months. But we've had an understanding that yours may well be the longest of the cases. On the other hand, Mr. Bakrac is taking on crime base to a certain extent on behalf of the VJ, which -- which makes his position not dissimilar in some respects to yours. It -- this is something you may not be willing to tell the Bench - and that's understandable - but if we were clear on whether or not Mr. Lukic was going to give evidence, it would assist us in -- in our own consideration of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to admit, Your Honour, that we are not clear on that yet either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, dividing the -- the balance of time, which was in fact 145 hours, even dividing it would take the Bakrac case to the end of January. So in spite of what Mr. Bakrac said to us before, we don't think it's a realistic submission that he has made to us and we were --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We were expecting to get this result today so that we can leave no doubt in his mind where he stands early enough, as -- as happened when we were in some doubt about where the Ojdanic Defence was going, to enable adequate arrangements to be made to ensure that the case was -- was fully presented. So if there's no agreement between you, then we will have to make an order. And therefore, if you want to make further submissions, we'll hear them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours, if you change the plan to finish this trial by the end of March or mid of April. If it's not changed, I'm sure that we'll easily fit into that schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. The -- using the -- bearing in mind the time that you're being -- that -- that the Chamber is not sitting, which on a number of occasions is for the convenience of the Defence. Taking account of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember too much of this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't remember the Orthodox New Year or Christmas arrangement? You don't remember the three months last year of -- after the end of the Prosecution case? Have you forgotten these?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I stand corrected. You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the situation between now and the spring, using every available minute, this evidence could not be completed on -- on the basis of 240 hours before approaching the end of April. And that's being realistic about the time for cross-examination and other issues. Not all time is taken up by examination and cross-examination, as you know, and indeed there's the issue of cross-examination by one accused of -- of the witnesses of the other.
